Lives · 1332–1406

Ibn Khaldun

History & Society · Tunis / Cairo · 1332–1406

3 min readWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 19 September 2026
On this pageWhere it is contestedCorrectedThe definitive biographyReads across to

He spent twenty years inside North African politics, then withdrew to a fortress and wrote down why dynasties fall.

If you keep one line

The cohesion that takes a city is the first thing the city spends.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332, into a family that had left Seville a century before. When he was about seventeen the Black Death killed both his parents. He went into government at twenty. For the next two decades he served, plotted against and fled a run of courts: Fez, where he spent nearly two years in prison; Granada, which sent him as envoy to Pedro the Cruel of Castile; Bougie, where he ran the government; then Tlemcen. In 1375 he withdrew to the fortress of Qal'at Ibn Salama, in what is now Algeria. There he wrote the introduction to a history of the world. The introduction is the part anyone still reads.

The Muqaddimah asks why dynasties rise and fall, and answers with 'asabiyya. Franz Rosenthal translated it as "group feeling"; it is closer to the solidarity of people who will fight for one another. Hard, cohesive groups from the desert take the cities, and the cities soften them. A generation, he reckoned, lasts forty years, and as a rule no dynasty outlasts three of them. The founders keep their cohesion. Their children keep a memory of it. The grandchildren forget to defend themselves. He called this a new science of human civilisation, and by his own note he drafted it in five months, finishing in November 1377.

The popular version has Europe rediscovering him. Ottoman scholars were there first. Kâtip Çelebi used his ages of the state to diagnose the empire's finances in 1653, and Pirizade translated five of the six chapters into Ottoman Turkish in the first half of the eighteenth century. The full Arabic text was not printed in Europe until Quatremère's Paris edition of 1858. His own last years were spent in Cairo, where he was made chief Maliki judge and dismissed, again and again. His wife and daughters drowned in 1384, when their ship went down on the way to join him. In the winter of 1400–01, with Damascus under siege, he was let down the city wall on ropes to meet Timur, and at the conqueror's request wrote him a description of North Africa. He died in Cairo in 1406.

01Where it is contested

Whether he founded sociology is the argument, and it is partly an argument about who gets to claim him. Ernest Gellner, whose own model of Muslim societies was built on him, treated him as a sociologist in all but name. Aziz Al-Azmeh, in 'Ibn Khaldun: An Essay in Reinterpretation' (2003), calls that anachronism: he was a Maliki jurist writing inside Islamic historiography, and there is no line of descent from him to Durkheim. Robert Irwin's biography leans to Al-Azmeh's side and warns against readers who find their own reflection in him. The taxation passage has the same problem on a smaller scale. "At the beginning of the dynasty, taxation yields a large revenue from small assessments," he wrote, and "at the end of the dynasty, taxation yields a small revenue from large assessments." Ronald Reagan quoted it at a press conference on 1 October 1981, and supply-side writers have claimed him as a forerunner of the Laffer curve ever since. Read in place, it describes how a dynasty's finances decay over a century, not a curve relating any tax rate to revenue at one moment; economists who have gone back to the text argue the two have little in common.

02Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 16 · Sept 2026 · Five quotations the house had not seen.

An audit of quotations checked each one against the document it comes from. Five could not be found in any document the house could open, so they are no longer printed in quotation marks: Confucius on not imposing on others (the translator was never named), Ibn Khaldun on dynasties lasting three generations (not found in the Rosenthal translation the entry relies on), Robert Moses's 'stein' statement (two wordings circulate, and the 1981 obituary that carries it could not be opened), Clair Patterson's 1966 testimony about the Public Health Service, and Thomas Blanton's line about Arkhipov. Each is now given as a paraphrase, which is what the colophon says an unquoted line is. None of them has been shown to be wrong. Separately, Tu Youyou's entry called Rao, Zhang and Li's book the only book-length account in English; Tu's own 2017 book covers the same discovery, as chemistry rather than history.

03The definitive biography

Ibn Khaldun: An Intellectual BiographyRobert Irwin · 2018

It reads him as what he was, a Maliki jurist and courtier writing inside Islamic historiography, and treats the Qur'anic citations as part of the argument rather than ornament. For his own words, go next to N. J. Dawood's one-volume abridgement of Rosenthal's translation; Rosenthal's three volumes (1958) are the reference, not the door.

Genghis Khan — the steppe-to-city cycle at its largest. Nearly two centuries later Ibn Khaldun sat across from Timur outside Damascus.
